summary: At Sinai God calls Moses into the cloud and commands him to record the divisions of time and the history that follows. God foresees Israel's covenant failure, scattering, return, and renewed sanctuary; Moses intercedes, and the angel of the presence receives the chronological tablets.
whyItMatters: The opening makes the whole book a Sinai revelation and places its ordered history inside a larger story of judgment, repentance, and divine dwelling.

context.author: Within the book, the angel of the presence dictates the account to Moses; the historical writer is unnamed.
context.audience: Israel is addressed through Moses in the book’s frame; the specific first historical audience is not identified.
context.date: The narrative places the revelation at Sinai; the historical Hebrew work is usually dated to the second century BCE, without an established exact year.
context.setting: Mount Sinai after the exodus, where Moses receives a vision that extends from creation toward a renewed Jerusalem.
context.literaryForm: Revelation frame with a divine forecast, Moses' prayer, and the commissioning of an angelic recorder.

before.text: The narrative opens at Sinai after the exodus, as Moses is summoned to receive the stone tablets and instruction.

here.text: The chapter frames the coming history as a written witness through Israel’s failure, return, and renewed dwelling with God.

after.text: The angel begins the dictated history with creation and the seventh day, showing why ordered time matters.

outline.heading: Moses enters the cloud
outline.note: The Sinai encounter introduces the law and the divisions of days.

outline.heading: A written witness against future rebellion
outline.note: God forecasts idolatry, captivity, and neglect of appointed times.

outline.heading: Return and dwelling promised
outline.note: The forecast turns toward renewed seeking and a sanctuary among the people.

outline.heading: Moses intercedes and God responds
outline.note: Moses asks for a clean heart; God promises a transformed people.

outline.heading: The angel receives the chronological tablets
outline.note: The narrated history is entrusted to the angel of the presence.

keyVerses.text: And Moses was on the Mount forty days and forty nights, and God taught him the earlier and the later history of the division of all the days of the law and of the testimony.
keyVerses.why: This verse makes the history of earlier and later days the subject of the Sinai instruction.

keyVerses.text: And after this they will turn to Me in all uprightness and with all (their) heart and with all (their) soul, and I will circumcise the foreskin of their heart and the foreskin of the heart of their seed, and I will create in them a holy spirit, and I will cleanse them so that they shall not turn away from Me from that day unto eternity.
keyVerses.why: The answer to Moses' prayer is a changed heart and durable covenant allegiance, not merely return from exile.

questions.question: Who is supposed to be speaking through the history that follows?
questions.answer: The chapter stages God speaking to Moses at Sinai and then instructing the angel of the presence to write for him. That is the book's narrative claim about its voice; it does not identify a historical writer outside the story.

questions.question: What are the “weeks and the jubilees”?
questions.answer: They are the ordered units of time by which the angelic record counts years and events. Verse 29 ties these divisions to the tablets, so chronology is part of the revelation rather than incidental date keeping.

questions.question: Why must Moses write down a warning about future failure?
questions.answer: God says the record will be a witness when Israel abandons the covenant after entering the land. The warning names practices and appointed times, and it also states that God has not permanently forsaken the people.

questions.question: Does the forecast mean Israel has no real responsibility for its choices?
questions.answer: The speech says God knows their rebellion in advance, but it still calls their worship and covenant breaches their own actions. Its purpose is to explain judgment and eventual return within the book, not to resolve every question about foreknowledge and freedom.

questions.question: What changes after the scattering among the Gentiles?
questions.answer: God promises that the people will seek him wholeheartedly, be gathered, and receive peace and a sanctuary in their midst. The sequence does not erase the earlier charges; it answers them with return and renewed relationship.

questions.question: Who or what is Beliar in Moses’ prayer?
questions.answer: Beliar is named as a hostile spirit that Moses fears may accuse and entrap the people. The chapter does not give a biography or a complete account of this figure, so the safest reading keeps to that role in the prayer.

questions.question: What does “circumcise the foreskin of their heart” mean here?
questions.answer: The image is explained by its own setting: God says he will create a holy spirit in them so they no longer turn away. It speaks of inward covenant change rather than describing a second physical procedure.

glossary.def: A recorded witness to what God commands and to the consequences of rejecting it.
The holy dwelling God says he will build among his people.
